old: Property rights are clearly defined, and the costs of negotiating and enforcing agreements are low.
new: Harm is reciprocal, and transaction costs are usually significant, so the zero-cost bargaining case is a benchmark rather than a description of most externalities.
why: Coase treated zero transaction costs as a hypothetical benchmark and stressed that real transaction costs are usually high, so presenting low costs as his assumption reverses his argument.

old: with low transaction costs, the efficient outcome can follow whoever holds the rights
new: with zero transaction costs, the efficient outcome follows whoever holds the rights; with positive costs, how rights are assigned matters
why: The Coase result holds under zero (not merely low) transaction costs, and Coase’s main point concerned the positive-cost case.

old: or allowing affected parties to bargain once property rights are clear
new: or comparing bargaining, legal rules and government action once transaction costs are taken into account
why: Coase 1960 argued for comparing institutional arrangements case by case, not for private bargaining as the general alternative to Pigouvian taxes.

old: Critics note that many externalities involve many parties, making bargaining costly or impractical.
new: Critics argue the analysis neglects how the initial assignment of rights affects distribution and fairness; the difficulty of bargaining among many parties was a point Coase himself stressed.
why: The many-parties objection was Coase’s own argument, so presenting it as a criticism of him misattributes positions.

old: Government can measure the external cost well enough to set a corrective tax or subsidy.
new: Government can measure the external cost well enough to set a corrective tax or subsidy, although Pigou himself warned that public authorities may lack the knowledge or independence to do so.
why: Pigou explicitly qualified his case with doubts about government competence, so the row should not imply naive faith in intervention.

old: Marshall’s consumer surplus
new: Marshall’s external economies
why: Pigou’s private–social divergence grew mainly from Marshall’s external economies (and Sidgwick), not from consumer surplus.

old: The chain traces Ricardo’s trade argument and its use in the Corn Law debate;
new: The chain traces Ricardo’s trade argument; his opposition to the Corn Laws, set out in 1815 before comparative advantage, rested mainly on his theory of rent and falling profits;
why: Ricardo’s anti-Corn Law case predates and does not derive from comparative advantage, so the chain otherwise implies a false causal sequence.

old: India’s post-1991 trade reforms, including the growth of services exports such as information technology, are often discussed using comparative advantage.
why: This is a generic application of a textbook concept rather than a genuine connection between Ricardo and India.

old: Institutional economics and political economy
new: New institutional economics and political economy
why: Institutional economics dates from Veblen and Commons in the 1890s–1920s; the 1970s span fits only the new institutional economics.

new: 1930s onwards
why: The Chicago school predates monetarism (Knight, Viner, Simons) and continued after the 1980s; only monetarism’s peak fits 1950s–1980s.

old: Written during the Great Depression and published in 1936, amid mass unemployment in Britain and elsewhere.
new: The 1931–32 exchange with Hayek concerned Keynes’s Treatise on Money (1930); the General Theory (1936), written amid mass unemployment, came later and Hayek never reviewed it in full.
why: The 1930s Hayek–Keynes debate centred on the Treatise on Money and Prices and Production, not on the 1936 General Theory.

old: Prices and wages adjust slowly; expectations and uncertainty can keep spending low for long periods.
new: Expectations and uncertainty can keep investment and spending low for long periods; even falling money wages need not restore full employment.
why: Keynes argued in the General Theory that flexible money wages would not reliably cure unemployment; sticky prices is the later neoclassical-synthesis reading.

old: Uncertainty and slow-adjusting wages and prices can leave demand too low for full employment.
new: Uncertainty and volatile expectations can leave demand too low for full employment, even if wages fall.
why: Attributing sticky wages and prices as the core Keynes assumption reflects later Keynesian models rather than the General Theory.

old: A postwar debate over
new: A postwar debate between Friedman and Keynesian economists, after Keynes’s death in 1946, over
why: Friedman’s critique targeted postwar Keynesian economics and demand management, not a debate with Keynes himself.

old: Critics point to inflation in the 1970s and doubts about how accurately governments can time intervention.
new: Critics point to 1970s inflation under postwar Keynesian policies, which went beyond Keynes’s own proposals, and to doubts about how accurately governments can time intervention.
why: Keynes died in 1946, so 1970s inflation is a criticism of later Keynesian policy rather than of Keynes directly.

old: scepticism about fine-tuning the economy with fiscal policy
new: scepticism about fine-tuning with either monetary or fiscal policy, given long and variable lags
why: Friedman’s case for a monetary rule rested on distrust of discretionary monetary as well as fiscal policy.

old: The steps follow Sen’s work from the 1980s to 1999; the HDI is a simplified measure
new: The steps follow Sen’s work from the late 1970s to 1999; the HDI (1990) predates Development as Freedom and is a simplified measure
why: The capability approach dates from Sen’s 1979 lecture and the HDI from 1990, so the chain order otherwise implies the HDI followed Development as Freedom.

old: This follows the order of Smith’s own argument in Book I.
new: The first four steps follow Smith’s argument in Book I; his case for freer trade is made mainly in Book IV.
why: The extent-of-the-market argument is Book I, chapter 3, but the trade case is in Book IV, so the note overstates.

old: draw directly on Keynesian reasoning
new: draw on Keynesian reasoning
why: Post-2008 and COVID-19 debates drew on many later models, so ‘directly’ overstates in the platform’s voice.

old: concepts she named
new: concepts she developed
why: The word monopsony was coined for her by Bertrand Hallward and price discrimination predates her, so ‘named’ overclaims.

old: critics accept the knowledge problem
new: many critics accept the knowledge problem
why: Not all critics accept it, so the unqualified statement is an absolute in the platform’s voice.

old: Argument against the Corn Laws
new: The classical case for free trade
why: Ricardo's opposition to the Corn Laws (1815) predates comparative advantage (1817), so placing it at the end of this chain implies a false sequence; added after review.
